q: Which of these is a Veblen good?
why: Its appeal comes from its high price: a pricier Rolex signals more status.

q: All Giffen goods are inferior goods. Are all inferior goods Giffen goods?
options: Yes, the two terms mean the same
No: a Giffen good must also have no close substitutes and take a big share of a poor household's budget
No, because Giffen goods are luxuries
why: Most inferior goods don't meet all three conditions, so they aren't Giffen goods.

q: A jewellery brand raises prices on its premium "heritage" line by 15%, and sales rise. The CFO calls it a lucky pricing mistake. What's the better explanation?
options: Demand for jewellery is perfectly elastic
It's a Giffen good, like bajra
The line behaves like a Veblen good: a higher price adds status
why: For status goods, the price is part of the appeal. The brand should check whether discounting would actually hurt this line.

q: Which causes a shift in the demand curve for tea?
why: Coffee's price is a non-price factor for tea, so tea's whole curve shifts right. A change in tea's own price is a movement along the curve.

q: An advertising campaign makes people want more of a soap at every price. What happens?
options: A movement along the demand curve
Nothing, since the price didn't change
why: Advertising changes tastes, a non-price factor, so the whole demand curve shifts.

q: A Kolkata sweet shop sells more rosogolla in October than in July at the same price. The owner credits his new signboard. What's the more likely explanation?
options: A movement along the demand curve
The festive season (Durga Puja) shifted the demand curve right
why: Same price, more sold: a non-price factor (festive demand, gifting) shifted the curve. The signboard may help, but the season matters more.

q: Price falls 5% and quantity demanded rises 15%. What's the price elasticity?
why: 15 ÷ 5 = 3. More than 1 means elastic.

q: Price drops from ₹6 to ₹4 and quantity rises from 10 to 15 units. Using the original price and quantity, what's the elasticity?
why: (Δq ÷ Δp) × (p ÷ q) = (5 ÷ 2) × (6 ÷ 10) = 1.5, so demand is elastic.

q: An airline and a salt company both plan a 10% price hike. Which should worry more about revenue?
options: The salt company, because salt is a necessity
Neither: a price rise always raises revenue
The airline, because air travel is elastic
why: Air travel has substitutes (trains) and trips can be postponed, so revenue likely falls. Salt is highly inelastic, so its revenue likely rises.

q: Income rises 10% and TV demand rises 20%. What type of good is a TV here?
why: Income elasticity = 20 ÷ 10 = 2. Above 1 means a luxury.

q: Income rises 5% and bajra demand falls 2%. What's the income elasticity?
why: −2 ÷ 5 = −0.4. Negative income elasticity means an inferior good.

q: After incomes rise 10%, a dealer's new-car sales go from 400 to 500 and used-car sales from 4,000 to 3,850. If incomes keep rising, what should the dealer stock more of?
options: Used cars, since they sell more units
Neither: income doesn't affect car sales
New cars: income elasticity 2.5, a luxury
why: New cars: +25% ÷ 10% = 2.5 (luxury). Used cars: −3.75% ÷ 10% = −0.375 (inferior). Rising incomes favour new cars.

q: The cross elasticity between two notebook brands is +1.5. What are they?
why: Positive cross elasticity means substitutes, and 1.5 is a strong reaction.

q: Printers are sold cheap, but ink cartridges are expensive. Which concept explains this?
why: Once you own the printer you need that brand's ink, so demand for the ink is inelastic and the company profits on it.

q: Kolkata metro fares are cut. Which business should worry more?
why: Metro rides substitute for cabs (positive cross elasticity), so cheaper metro fares cut cab demand. Tea stalls near stations are closer to complements: more riders, more footfall.

q: Opportunity cost is…
options: The total value of all your options
The value of the next-best option you give up
why: Only your next-best option counts, not every option you skipped.

q: Rahul leaves a ₹6 lakh-a-year job for a 2-year MBA with ₹10 lakh in fees. What's the full economic cost?
why: ₹10 lakh fees + ₹12 lakh salary given up over 2 years = ₹22 lakh.

q: A company can spend ₹50 crore on a new factory or on a marketing campaign. It picks the factory. What is the campaign's expected return?
options: The opportunity cost of building the factory
Irrelevant once the choice is made
why: The factory only makes sense if its expected return beats the campaign's.

q: A point inside the PPF shows…
why: Resources are sitting idle (unemployment, unused machines), so more of both goods is possible.

q: Which of these shifts India's PPF outward?
why: A strike moves production inside the curve. Using idle machines moves it towards the curve, not beyond it.

q: A textile firm's machines run at 60% capacity, yet the CEO wants to build a new plant. What should you ask first?
options: Why not use the 40% idle capacity first?
How much will the new plant cost?
why: The firm is inside its own PPF. A new plant only makes sense if demand will outgrow even full capacity.

q: Which of these causes a shift in the supply curve?
why: Lower costs shift supply right. A price change is a movement along the curve, and incomes shift demand, not supply.

q: The government gives solar-panel makers a subsidy. What happens to supply?
why: Lower costs mean more is supplied at every price.

q: A Kolkata flower seller can't increase supply during Durga Puja even though prices triple. Why?
options: Perishable, seasonal goods have nearly fixed supply in the short run
The law of supply doesn't apply to flowers
why: With supply fixed in the short run, a demand spike becomes a price spike.

q: If the price is set above equilibrium, there will be…
why: At a high price, sellers offer more than buyers want, so stock piles up.

q: A heatwave raises demand for ACs while a GST cut makes them cheaper to supply. What happens to the quantity sold?
why: Demand ↑ and supply ↑ both push quantity up. The price effect is unclear, since the two forces pull price in opposite directions.

q: A new café's ₹49 cold coffee has a 30-minute queue every evening. What's the economic signal?
options: The price is below equilibrium: a shortage
The price is above equilibrium: a surplus
why: Buyers want more than the café supplies at ₹49. It can raise the price, add capacity, or treat the queue as free marketing.

q: Total utility after 3 cups is 65 and after 4 cups is 75. What's the marginal utility of the 4th cup?
why: MU = TU₄ − TU₃ = 75 − 65 = 10.

q: When marginal utility becomes negative, total utility…
why: Each extra unit now subtracts satisfaction, so the total drops.

q: A pizza chain offers "second pizza at 50% off". Which concept explains the discount?
why: The second pizza is worth less to you, so the chain lowers its price to match what you'd pay.

q: Why are indifference curves convex to the origin?
options: Because of the law of supply
Because of a diminishing marginal rate of substitution (MRS)
why: You give up less and less of one good for each extra unit of the other.

q: How does the indifference curve approach treat utility?
why: It only ranks combinations as better, worse or equal, without measuring utility.

q: A student spends all her pocket money on chai and samosas. Chai's price doubles. What happens?
options: Her budget line shifts out and she's happier
Nothing changes, since her income is the same
Her budget line pivots inward on the chai side, and she moves to a lower indifference curve
why: She can no longer afford her old mix, so she ends up on a lower curve and most likely buys fewer chais.

q: A student wants an iPhone but can't afford one. Is this demand?
options: No: it's a want without purchasing power
Yes, because the student is a customer
why: Demand is a want backed by the ability and willingness to pay.

q: A bank launches easy EMIs for two-wheelers. What is it doing?
options: Turning wants into demand by increasing purchasing power
why: EMIs let people who want a two-wheeler actually afford one.

q: A premium gym in Kolkata gets thousands of Instagram likes but few sign-ups. What's the likely gap?
options: High want, low demand: people like it but can't or won't pay
why: Fixes include trial passes, monthly plans and student pricing.

q: Customer value is…
why: Value is judged by the customer: what they get versus everything they give up.

q: Which of these is a non-money cost of shopping at a crowded mall on a Sunday?
why: Customers also pay in time, effort and stress, not just money.

q: A café raises coffee prices by ₹20 but adds free Wi-Fi and charging points, and student footfall rises. Why?
options: Perceived benefits rose more than perceived costs, so value went up
why: For students who study there, a work-friendly space is worth more than the extra ₹20.

q: When performance exceeds expectations, the customer feels…
why: Below expectations → dissatisfied. Equal → satisfied. Above → delighted.

q: A customer brings ₹200 profit per purchase, buys twice a month and stays 2 years. What's their lifetime value (before adjustments)?
why: ₹200 × 2 purchases × 24 months = ₹9,600.

q: An app's ads promise "delivery in 10 minutes, every time", but it averages 18 minutes, still faster than most rivals. Customers are angry. Why?
options: Satisfaction compares performance with expectations, and the ad set them at 10 minutes
why: Over-promising raises expectations, so even good performance feels like failure.

q: "Consumers won't buy enough unless they're persuaded." Which orientation is this?
why: The selling concept relies on aggressive promotion rather than on what customers need.

q: A phone brand adds a 200 MP camera, but its buyers care more about battery life. Which trap is this?
options: Product orientation, leading to marketing myopia
why: A superior feature isn't a superior value proposition if customers don't value it.

q: A paint company says it's in "the paint business". What's a non-myopic way to define it?
options: We make paint in many colours
We help people create beautiful, lasting homes
why: Defining the business by the customer's need opens up waterproofing, décor, painting services and design consultation.

q: Competitors are part of a company's…
why: Micro = nearby actors (suppliers, intermediaries, customers, competitors, publics). Macro = broad forces like PESTLE.

q: Rising edible-oil prices hit an FMCG company. Which is a sensible marketing response?
options: Ignore it, since it's a macro factor
why: Other responses from the notes: raise prices or revise promotions.

q: A fashion app uses location, browsing and purchase history to personalise ads. Under India's DPDP law, what must it do?
options: Nothing: the data belongs to the app
Get clear, informed consent with proper notice, and protect the data
why: Personalisation is still possible, but it must be built on consent; breaches must also be reported.

q: Which force is strong when switching costs are low and information is easy to find?
why: Buyers can compare and switch easily, so they can push prices down.

q: Only two companies in the world make an advanced chip that phone makers need. Which force is strong?
why: Few suppliers of a critical, hard-to-replace input means strong supplier power.

q: A coffee chain tracks only other coffee chains as competitors. What is it missing?
options: Substitutes that meet the same need: tea, energy drinks, a place to hang out
why: Its real competitive set is defined by the customer's need, which is much broader than coffee chains.

q: Low involvement + significant brand differences = ?
why: Buyers switch brands just to try something new.

q: For habitual products like salt, what matters most to the marketer?
why: Wide distribution, distinctive packaging and repetition keep the brand the default pick.

q: Many customers cancel an insurance policy within 15 days of buying it. Which buying type is this, and what's the fix?
options: Dissonance-reducing: reassure customers after the purchase
why: Policies look similar, so buyers doubt their choice afterwards. A welcome call, a clear benefits summary and testimonials help.

q: Researching online, then buying in a store, is called…
why: Showrooming is the reverse: look in the store, buy online.

q: A buyer rejects every laptop under 16 GB RAM, however good its other features. Which evaluation rule is this?
why: A strength elsewhere can't make up for failing the cut-off.

q: A product page gets lots of traffic but few sales. Where should you look first?
options: Evaluation and purchase: price vs rivals, reviews, stock, EMI, delivery
why: Traffic shows interest. Something is blocking the final step.

q: A hospital reorders the same gloves from the same supplier every month. Which buying situation is this?
why: A routine reorder with no change in supplier or specs is a straight rebuy.

q: Demand for steel rises because car sales are booming. What is this?
why: Business demand depends on demand from end consumers.

q: A company's sales head loves your CRM demo, but the deal stalls for months. Who should you engage?
options: Only the sales head, more often
IT (influencer and gatekeeper), finance (approver) and procurement (buyer)
why: In B2B, many people decide. Winning the user isn't enough.

q: The upper limit of industry sales as marketing effort becomes very large is called…
why: Your sales forecast is your realistic share; market potential is the ceiling for the whole industry.

q: 10,000 households × 20% buy × 4 packs a year × ₹100. What's the market size?
Two consultants give very different market sizes for the same product. What should you check first?
options: Their definitions: product scope, customers, geography and time period
why: Most gaps come from defining different markets, for example a financial year versus a calendar year.

q: "Why do first-time users not return?" What's the best first research method?
why: Qualitative research uncovers the why. A survey can then size how many people feel that way.

q: Which landing page converts better, A or B? What's the best method?
why: Show each version to a random half of visitors and compare conversions.

q: "Our survey of 5,000 Instagram followers shows 90% love the new flavour, so let's launch nationally." What's wrong?
options: Sampling bias: followers already like the brand
why: A large but biased sample can still be confidently wrong.

q: A shopping app adds an item you didn't choose to your cart. Which dark pattern is this?
why: Basket sneaking is one of the 13 dark patterns banned in India's 2023 guidelines.

q: A brand says "eco-friendly packaging" with no details or evidence. What's the issue?
why: Green claims must be specific and backed by evidence.

q: A fitness creator praises a protein powder without saying the brand paid them ₹50,000. What's the fix?
options: Delete the post after a week
Add a clear "#ad / paid partnership" label at the start
Mention it only in the comments
why: Undisclosed paid promotion misleads followers into thinking it's an independent opinion.

q: Maximum usage is 40 units a day and maximum lead time is 4 days. What's the reorder level?
why: Reorder level = maximum usage × maximum lead time = 40 × 4 = 160.

q: Reorder level is 500 units, normal usage is 60 units a week and normal lead time is 5 weeks. What's the minimum level?
why: Minimum level = reorder level − (normal usage × normal lead time) = 500 − 300 = 200.

q: Shipping delays add two weeks to an importer's lead time. What should it do first?
options: Cut its safety stock to save cash
Raise its reorder level and safety stock, accepting more working capital
why: A longer lead time means ordering earlier to avoid stockouts. The cost is more cash tied up, so it should also look for nearer or second suppliers.

q: At the economic order quantity (EOQ), how do yearly ordering costs compare with yearly holding costs?
why: EOQ is the balance point where the two costs are equal and their total is lowest.

q: Annual demand is 800 units, each order costs ₹100 and holding one unit for a year costs ₹4. What's the EOQ?
A supplier offers a 5% discount if you order 1,000 units at a time, well above your EOQ of 300. How do you decide?
options: Compare total annual cost both ways: purchase price + ordering + holding
Order the average of the two
why: EOQ ignores discounts. Take the bulk order only if the price saving beats the extra holding cost, and you have the space and cash.

q: Under FIFO, closing stock is valued at…
why: The oldest units go to cost of sales first, so the units left are the newest ones.

q: Opening stock is 50 units at ₹20; you buy 50 more at ₹30, then issue 60 units. What's the cost of the issue under FIFO?
why: FIFO uses the old stock first: 50 × ₹20 + 10 × ₹30 = ₹1,300.

q: Inflation is high, and a CFO in India wants to switch to LIFO to cut taxes. What do you tell her?
options: Go ahead: LIFO is the standard method
LIFO isn't allowed under Ind AS 2 / AS 2; choose FIFO or weighted average
Use LIFO only for tax returns
why: Indian accounting standards permit FIFO or weighted average, not LIFO. Weighted average smooths price swings.

q: In ABC analysis, A items are roughly…
options: Equal shares of items and value
why: A few high-value items hold most of the money, so they get the tightest control.

q: An item is 5% of the number of items but 60% of the value. Which ABC category is it?
options: It depends on its price per unit
why: A small share of items with a large share of value is the definition of an A item.

q: A ₹50 sensor runs out and stops a whole production line. What did the company's ABC-only system miss?
options: Criticality: a cheap item can be vital, so add a VED check
why: ABC ranks by value only. VED (Vital, Essential, Desirable) flags cheap items that can still stop production.

q: The inventory turnover ratio is…
options: Cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory
why: It shows how many times stock is sold and replaced in a year. Inventory days = 365 ÷ turnover.

q: Opening stock is ₹30,000, closing stock ₹50,000, and cost of goods sold ₹2,40,000. What's the inventory turnover?
why: Average inventory = ₹40,000, so turnover = 2,40,000 ÷ 40,000 = 6 times (about 61 days).

q: Two grocery chains have the same sales. Chain X turns its stock 12 times a year, chain Y 6 times. What does that tell an investor?
options: X needs about half as much cash tied up in stock
why: X holds about 30 days of stock versus Y's 61, so it can fund growth more cheaply. Y may be overstocked.

q: Under a piece rate system, wages depend on…
why: Piece rate pays per unit, which rewards speed but needs quality checks.

q: A worker's normal day is 8 hours at ₹80 an hour. She works 10 hours, with overtime at 1.5 times the normal rate. What are her total wages?
Standard time is 12 hours, a worker takes 9 hours, and the rate is ₹60 an hour. Which plan pays her more?
why: Time wages ₹540. Halsey bonus = 50% × 3 × 60 = ₹90. Rowan bonus = (3 ÷ 12) × 9 × 60 = ₹135. She saved less than half the standard time, so Rowan pays more.

q: The separation method divides the number of people who left by…
why: Average workers = (start + end) ÷ 2. The result is multiplied by 100.

q: Average workers are 200 and 50 people left in the year. What's labour turnover by the separation method?
A factory starts the year with 80 workers and ends with 120. 10 people left and 6 were replaced. What's the flux rate?
why: Average = 100, so flux = (10 + 6) ÷ 100 × 100 = 16%. It shows total churn: exits plus refills.

q: The routine, clerical recording of every transaction is called…
why: Book-keeping is the recording step. Accounting summarises and interprets; accountancy is the whole body of knowledge.

q: The canteen wants to know what each plate of biryani really costs to make. Which branch of accounting helps most?
why: Cost accounting works out the cost of products, jobs and departments, and how to reduce it.

q: A bank is deciding whether to lend ₹50 lakh to a small firm. What kind of user is the bank, and what will it focus on?
options: An internal user, focused on employee morale
An external user (lender), focused on the firm's ability to repay
An internal user, focused on product design
why: Lenders look at cash flows, existing debt, security available and steady profits.

q: Which equation is the foundation of double-entry book-keeping?
why: Everything a business owns is financed by outsiders (liabilities) or the owner (capital).

q: A firm has assets of ₹2,00,000 and liabilities of ₹80,000. What is the owner's capital?
why: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = ₹2,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹1,20,000.

q: A firm pays ₹5,000 salary in cash. What happens to the accounting equation?
why: Cash (an asset) goes down, and the expense reduces the owner's capital, so the equation stays balanced.

q: Which statement shows a company's financial position on a particular date?
why: The balance sheet is a snapshot "as at" a date; the P&L covers a period.

q: How would you classify a patent, a fixed deposit and a delivery van?
why: A patent can't be touched (intangible), a deposit is a financial asset, and a van is tangible.

q: A company reports record profit, but its cash fell and trade receivables doubled. What's the most likely explanation?
options: It sold on credit and isn't collecting cash fast enough
It paid off all its loans
why: Profit is recorded when sales are made, but the cash is still with customers. Profit isn't the same as cash.

q: "The business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future." Which concept is this?
why: Because the business is expected to continue, assets are spread over their useful life, not valued at fire-sale prices.

q: The owner takes ₹10,000 of stock home for personal use. How is it treated?
why: Under the business entity concept, the owner's personal use is drawings, not a business expense.

q: A start-up's founder wants to record the "value" of a newly hired star manager as a ₹10 lakh asset. Is that allowed?
options: No: under money measurement, only transactions measured in money are recorded
why: The manager's talent wasn't bought as an asset. The salary is an expense.

q: Assets are recorded at their purchase price, not at today's market value. Which concept is this?
why: The original cost is the basis for all later accounting for the asset.

q: March's rent of ₹20,000 is paid on 5 April. The year ends on 31 March. When is it an expense?
options: In the year ending 31 March, as an outstanding expense
In the next year, when it's paid
It's split between the two years
why: Under accrual, expenses are recorded when incurred, not when paid.

q: A coaching institute collects ₹1,20,000 in January for a 12-month course starting 1 January. Its year ends 31 March. How much revenue should it record for the year?
why: Only 3 months are delivered (3 × ₹10,000). The other ₹90,000 is income received in advance, a liability.

q: Valuing stock at the lower of cost or net realisable value follows which convention?
why: Conservatism (prudence) provides for likely losses but doesn't book unrealised gains.

q: A company switches its depreciation method every year to smooth its profits. Which convention does it break?
why: Methods should stay the same from year to year so results can be compared.

q: A company faces a ₹50 crore lawsuit it may or may not lose. The CFO wants to leave it out of the annual report. What do you advise?
options: Leave it out until the case ends
Record the full ₹50 crore as a liability now
Disclose it as a contingent liability in the notes
why: Full disclosure requires material uncertainties to be shown. If a loss becomes probable and can be estimated, provide for it.

q: Under the modern rules, an increase in an expense is recorded as a…
why: Increases in assets and expenses are debits; increases in liabilities, capital and incomes are credits.

q: The stall pays ₹10,000 cash to Mondal Traders, a creditor. What's the journal entry?
why: The liability to Mondal Traders falls (debit) and cash, an asset, falls (credit).

q: A business takes a ₹5 lakh bank loan, credited to its bank account. Which accounts are debited and credited?
why: Bank, an asset, rises (debit). The loan, a liability, rises (credit).

q: Which error does NOT affect the agreement of the trial balance?
options: Posting a debit to the wrong side
A wrong total in the purchases book
Debiting an asset purchase to an expense account
Posting only one side of an entry
why: An error of principle puts the right amount on the right side, just in the wrong kind of account, so totals still agree.

q: The trial balance's debit side is ₹500 more than the credit side, and the error can't be found yet. What do you do?
options: Credit ₹500 to a suspense account until the error is found
Write it off as a loss
why: Suspense is a temporary account that makes the totals agree until the error is located and rectified.

q: A ₹2,000 credit sale to Mr Sen is completely left out of the books. What happens?
options: The trial balance agrees, but sales, debtors and profit are understated by ₹2,000
Only the cash book is wrong
why: A complete omission affects neither side, so the totals still match, yet the books are wrong.

q: A credit purchase of goods for resale is first recorded in the…
why: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods the business deals in.

q: Where is a cash sale of goods recorded?
why: The sales book is only for credit sales; cash transactions go to the cash book.

q: A petty cashier holds an imprest of ₹5,000 and spends ₹4,200 in the month. How much does the main cashier give her at month-end?
why: Under the imprest system, the exact amount spent is reimbursed, restoring the fixed float of ₹5,000.

q: A supply of goods from West Bengal to Odisha attracts which GST?
why: Inter-state supplies attract IGST; supplies within a state attract CGST + SGST.

q: Input GST paid on purchases is ₹18,000 and output GST charged on sales is ₹27,000. How much does the business pay the government?
why: Input tax credit is set off against output tax: ₹27,000 − ₹18,000 = ₹9,000.

q: Why isn't GST paid on purchases added to the cost of inventory?
options: Because it's recovered as input tax credit against GST on sales, so it's an asset, not a cost
Because inventory is always valued at selling price
why: Adding recoverable GST to inventory would overstate costs and double-count the tax.

q: Ordinary repairs to keep a machine running are…
why: They maintain existing earning capacity and their benefit is used up within the period.

q: Legal fees paid to buy a plot of land are…
options: Capital expenditure, part of the land's cost
why: Costs needed to acquire an asset are part of the asset's cost.

q: An old fridge with a book value of ₹8,000 is sold for ₹10,000. What goes to the profit and loss account?
why: The ₹10,000 is a capital receipt; only the profit on sale (₹10,000 − ₹8,000) is credited to the P&L.

q: How is a contingent liability shown in the accounts?
options: Recorded as a liability in the balance sheet
Disclosed in the notes to accounts
why: It's only a possible obligation (or not probable or measurable), so it's disclosed, not recorded, unless it's remote.

q: A company guarantees a bank loan taken by another company. For the guarantor, this is…
why: The guarantor pays only if the borrower defaults, an uncertain future event.

q: A lawsuit once thought unlikely to succeed now looks likely to cost about ₹10 lakh. What changes?
options: Nothing; keep it in the notes
Record a ₹10 lakh provision, as the outflow is now probable and measurable
Record it as a contingent asset
why: When an outflow becomes probable and can be reliably estimated, a contingent liability becomes a provision.

q: Which companies must follow Ind AS?
options: Listed companies, NBFCs and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more
why: Other companies follow the Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021.

q: Which is a valid reason to change an accounting policy?
options: To show higher profit this year
It's required by law or an accounting standard, or gives a more appropriate presentation
why: Policy changes need a valid reason, and their effect must be quantified and disclosed.

q: A company decides its machines will last 8 years instead of 5. What kind of change is this?
options: A change in accounting estimate, applied from now on
why: Useful life is a judgement within the depreciation method, so revising it is an estimate change, applied prospectively.

q: Inventories are generally measured at…
options: The lower of cost and net realisable value
why: Realisable value caps inventory for prudence: never above what it can be sold for.

q: A machine costs ₹7,00,000 plus ₹1,00,000 for installation. What's its historical cost?
why: Historical cost includes everything needed to get the asset ready for use.

q: A bank bought a bond for ₹100. Yields rose and its market price is now ₹96. If the bank measures it at market value, what does it report?
why: Measuring at current market value means unrealised price falls show up as losses.

q: Under the straight line method, the depreciation charge is…
why: SLM = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, charged equally each year.

q: Cost ₹1,00,000, residual value ₹10,000, useful life 9 years. What's the annual SLM depreciation?
A company's laptops lose most of their value in the first two years. Which depreciation method fits better?
options: Written down value, which charges more early
why: WDV front-loads depreciation, matching assets that lose value fast through obsolescence.

q: How many parties does a bill of exchange generally have?
options: Four: drawer, drawee, payee and bank
why: A promissory note has two parties; a bill has three.

q: A bill dated 1 March is payable 2 months after date. When does it mature?
why: The due date is 1 May, plus 3 days of grace = 4 May.

q: A ₹1,00,000 three-month bill is discounted at a bank at 12% a year. Roughly how much does the holder receive?
why: Discount = ₹1,00,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹3,000, so the holder receives about ₹97,000 now instead of waiting.

q: Fred Luthans described OB as being concerned with which three things?
options: Understanding, predicting and controlling human behaviour
why: OB aims to understand, predict and shape how people behave at work, so managers can improve results.

q: A company studies why its Tokyo and Kolkata offices have very different meeting cultures. Which discipline is OB borrowing from most?
why: Anthropology studies cultures and how they shape behaviour.

q: A startup loses 40% of new hires within six months. The founder says it's purely about salary. What would an OB view do first?
options: Check all three levels: the person's fit, how teams treat newcomers, and the culture
why: OB looks at individual, group and organisation causes before assuming one explanation.

q: In Lewin's equation B = f(P, E), what does E stand for?
why: Behaviour depends on the person and the environment around them: boss, team, rules and rewards.

q: TCS linked variable pay to office attendance in 2024 and attendance rose. Which part of Lewin's equation did it change?
why: It changed the environment (rewards), and behaviour followed, without changing people's personalities.

q: A star salesperson becomes average after moving from Kolkata to Delhi. What does Lewin's equation suggest?
options: Look at both a changed environment (manager, market, team) and the person (stress of moving)
Salespeople never succeed after a transfer
why: Behaviour is a function of person AND environment, so check both before judging.

q: Which OB model rests on economic resources like pensions and benefits?
why: The custodial model buys security and loyalty with benefits, but it creates dependence, not drive.

q: A startup treats employees as partners and involves them in product decisions. Which model is this?
why: The collegial model is built on partnership and shared responsibility.

q: A factory pays well and offers housing, but workers do the bare minimum and never suggest ideas. What's the best diagnosis?
options: An autocratic model; fire the slow workers
A system model that's working perfectly
A custodial model with no supportive leadership; add recognition and involvement
why: Benefits create security but only passive cooperation. Recognition and involvement build motivation.

q: Who is most associated with bureaucracy, a hierarchy run by written rules?
why: Weber argued that rational-legal rules beat decisions based on personal favours.

q: A manager says: there's no single best way to manage; it depends on our market and technology. Which school is this?
why: Contingency theory says the right approach depends on the situation.

q: A call centre doubles output by scripting and timing every call, but attrition hits 60%. Which pair best explains this?
options: Bureaucracy drove the gain; systems theory drove attrition
Scientific management drove the gain; ignoring human relations drove the attrition
why: Taylor-style efficiency raised output, but ignoring workers' needs for recognition and autonomy made people quit.

q: In OB, what does 'coping with temporariness' refer to?
options: Managing constant change: gig and contract workers, reorganisations and fast-ageing skills
why: Work is less permanent today, so managers must build engagement with people who may not stay long.

q: A bank lets branch staff approve small loans without head-office sign-off. Which challenge is it responding to?
why: Empowerment pushes decisions down to the people closest to the customer.

q: The 2025 Union Budget promised ID cards, e-Shram registration and health cover for about 1 crore gig workers. Which OB challenge does this reflect most?
options: Coping with temporariness: people who work for platforms without being employees
why: Gig workers are a growing, non-permanent workforce, which is the temporariness challenge.

q: Which Big Five trait best predicts job performance across most jobs?
why: Organised, dependable and persistent people tend to perform better in almost every role.

q: A trading-desk role needs calm decisions under pressure. Which trait should be LOW?
why: Low neuroticism means high emotional stability, which suits high-pressure roles.

q: A firm hires salespeople only if their MBTI type is ENTJ, and results don't improve. Why?
options: The MBTI predicts job performance poorly; Big Five traits plus structured interviews work better
They should have hired only introverts
why: The MBTI is useful for self-awareness but weak at predicting performance.

q: In Freud's model, which part acts as our conscience?
why: The superego holds the rules and values learned from parents and society.

q: A manager scolded by the boss goes back and snaps at a junior. Which defence mechanism is this?
why: Displacement moves anger to a safer target.

q: SEBI found 93% of individual F&O traders lost money over FY22–FY24, yet over 75% of loss-makers kept trading. Which Freudian idea best explains 'I was just unlucky, next time will be different'?
options: Defence mechanisms like rationalisation and denial
why: Excuses and denial protect self-image, so people repeat the behaviour instead of learning.

q: According to Bandura, what is the strongest source of self-efficacy?
options: Your own past successes at the task
why: Mastery experiences, actually succeeding, build task confidence most.

q: An employee says: promotions here are just politics, so why try? This shows…
why: Externals believe outside forces decide results, and may slide into learned helplessness.

q: A new joinee is scared of client presentations. Which plan best builds her self-efficacy?
options: Tell her confidence can't be learned
Put her in front of the biggest client on day one
Small internal presentations first, watch a peer, specific encouragement and rehearsal
why: This uses all four of Bandura's sources: mastery, modelling, persuasion and managing emotions.

q: What are the three middle stages of the perception process?
why: We choose what to notice, group it into patterns, then give it meaning.

q: A bright red '50% OFF' sign stands out on a street of plain boards. Which factors make it noticed?
options: Target factors: intensity, size, novelty and contrast
why: Features of the target itself grab attention.

q: Ola Electric said it resolved 99.1% of 10,644 complaints, yet many buyers still saw its service as poor. What does this show about perception?
options: Past experience shapes interpretation; once formed, perceptions filter new information
why: Perceiver factors like experience and expectations colour how people read new facts.

q: What is the fundamental attribution error?
options: Blaming others' behaviour on their personality and underestimating the situation
why: We tend to explain other people's failures by who they are, not by what they faced.

q: A salesperson says: I hit target because I'm brilliant; I missed last quarter because the market was bad. This is…
why: Credit for success goes inside, blame for failure goes outside.

q: All five branch managers in one region missed their loan targets. In attribution terms, what does this point to?
options: Low distinctiveness, so fire them all
High consistency, so it's the managers' fault
High consensus, so look for an external cause like the region's economy or the targets
why: When everyone in the same situation behaves the same way, the cause is likely external.

q: What is the halo effect?
options: Forming an overall impression from a single trait
Judging someone against the person before them
why: One strong trait, like a famous college or great speaking, colours the whole judgement.

q: An average candidate seems excellent because the two before her were poor. Which shortcut is this?
why: We compare with whoever came just before, not with a fixed standard.

q: A manager is told one trainee is 'a topper', gives him the best projects, and he shines while an equally able trainee stays average. Which effect is this?
why: Expectations changed the opportunities, which made the expectation come true.

q: What is eustress?
options: Positive, moderate stress that energises and improves performance
why: Some pressure sharpens focus; that's the top of the inverted-U curve.

q: A team with no deadlines and no targets keeps underperforming. Where is it on the stress curve?
options: The low end: too little challenge, so boredom
why: Too little stress means low arousal and low performance.

q: Analysts on 80-hour weeks improved for a fortnight, but now errors and resignations are climbing. What happened?
options: Stress has no link to performance
They crossed from eustress into distress
why: Sustained overload pushed them past the peak of the curve, so performance fell.

q: What are the three categories of stress symptoms?
why: Stress shows in the mind, the body and what people do.

q: An employee reports to two bosses who give opposite instructions. Which stressor is this?
why: Clashing expectations from a role are role conflict, an organisational stressor.

q: After a merger, staff don't know their new reporting lines and absenteeism doubles. What is the stressor, and what is the symptom?
why: Unclear roles cause stress, and absenteeism is a behavioural sign of it.

q: What is cognitive restructuring?
options: Changing negative thought patterns into more realistic ones
why: Reframing 'I'll fail' into 'this is tough but doable' reduces stress.

q: A company lets employees choose how they complete their tasks. Which stressor does this reduce?
why: More control over your own work lowers stress.

q: A bank offers free gym memberships, but stress surveys don't improve because targets change every week. What's missing?
options: Organisational action on the real stressor: stable, realistic targets
why: Individual perks can't fix an organisational stressor at its source.

q: What is the key performance difference between a work group and a work team?
options: Groups have a leader, teams don't
Teams create positive synergy: more than the sum of individual efforts
why: Shared goals, complementary skills and mutual accountability create synergy.

q: Employees from many departments join a 'Save Our Canteen' campaign. What type of group is it?
why: It formed on its own around a shared cause, outside the formal structure.

q: In 2024, Samsung Chennai workers formed a union and struck for 37 days for pay and recognition. In OB terms, what had formed?
options: An interest group of employees pursuing a shared goal
why: Interest groups form around a common objective, often outside the formal structure.

q: In Tuckman's model, in which stage do roles and rules become settled?
why: After storming, the group agrees norms and roles, and closeness grows.

q: A 6-week task force does little for 3 weeks, then suddenly rethinks its whole approach. Which model explains this?
why: Temporary groups often have a burst of change at the midpoint after a phase of inertia.

q: After Vistara merged into Air India in November 2024, two sets of crews had to work as one. Which stage should leaders expect early on?
options: Forming and storming over roles, rules and culture
why: A combined group must form and work through conflict before it can perform.

q: What is social loafing?
options: Putting in less effort in a group when individual contribution can't be seen
why: Hidden effort invites people to coast on others' work.

q: Which combination gives the LOWEST productivity?
why: A tight group that values slacking defends low output together.

q: A close-knit sales team agrees to 'never exceed target, or management will raise it'. What's the fix?
options: Change the norms: reward beating target and don't punish success with higher targets
why: Cohesion amplifies norms, so change the norm, not the closeness.

q: What is groupshift?
options: A group's position becoming more extreme than members' starting views after discussion
why: Discussion can push groups to riskier, or more cautious, positions than individuals held.

q: Which technique has members write ideas silently, present them one by one, then vote privately?
why: It stops one loud voice from dominating the decision.

q: An FAA panel found Boeing employees hesitant to raise safety concerns for fear of retaliation. Which group danger does silence like this feed?
why: When people self-censor, the organisation loses the dissent that catches errors.

q: Which team type takes over many of a supervisor's duties?
why: Self-managed teams plan, schedule and control their own work.

q: A bank brings together IT, compliance, marketing and branch staff to launch a UPI feature. Which team type?
why: People at similar levels from different departments combine expertise.

q: A team spread across Kolkata, Pune and Singapore keeps missing handovers and members feel like strangers. What fixes fit best?
options: Regular video check-ins, clear handover owners, overlapping hours and occasional meet-ups
why: Virtual teams need deliberate structure and social bonding.

q: What are the three groups of factors in Robbins' team effectiveness model?
why: Resources and rewards (context), the right members (composition) and how they work (process).

q: A talented team fails because everyone is rewarded only for individual targets. Which factor is broken?
options: Context: rewards don't recognise team contribution
why: Team-based evaluation and rewards are part of the context.

q: Which kind of conflict generally HELPS a team's decisions?
why: Debating ideas improves decisions; personal clashes hurt the team.

q: Under Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, a contract is…
options: A written document signed by both sides
An offer that has been made
why: Contract = agreement + enforceability. Writing helps prove it but isn't the test.

q: A husband promises his wife a monthly allowance, then stops paying. Can she sue on the promise?
options: Yes, if the amount is above ₹10,000
No, domestic promises usually lack intention to create legal relations (Balfour v Balfour)
why: Social and domestic agreements are generally not meant to be legally binding.

q: Two founders agree on WhatsApp to split profits 50:50 but sign nothing. One later denies it. What must the other prove?
options: That there was an enforceable contract: clear offer, acceptance, intention to be bound and consideration
Nothing, WhatsApp chats are always contracts
That the chat was over 100 words
why: Messages can be evidence, but the court asks whether a real, enforceable contract was formed.

q: What does 'consensus ad idem' mean?
options: A contract signed before a judge
A meeting of minds: both agree on the same thing in the same sense
why: Section 13: consent means agreeing on the same thing in the same sense.

q: A 16-year-old signs a ₹30,000 phone EMI agreement. Which essential is missing?
why: A minor can't contract, so the agreement is void.

q: In Dec 2024 the Supreme Court refused to let a consumer forum cap credit-card interest at 30%. Which reasoning did it rely on?
options: Courts can't rewrite terms freely agreed by the parties; rate regulation is the RBI's job
why: Freely agreed, lawful terms are generally enforced; the regulator sets rate rules.

q: Which case held that a public advertisement can be a general offer accepted by performance?
options: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
why: Mrs Carlill accepted by using the smoke ball as directed; she didn't need to write back.

q: A seller offers his bike for ₹40,000 and the buyer replies '₹35,000, final'. What is the buyer's reply?
options: A counter offer that rejects the original offer
why: Changing the terms kills the original offer and makes a new one.

q: A coaching centre advertises ₹10,000 to any student scoring 99 percentile after its course, then refuses a student who did. Best argument for the student?
options: It was a general offer accepted by performance, so the centre is bound
why: Like Carlill, meeting the advertised conditions accepts the offer.

q: Why was there no contract in Harvey v Facey?
options: A statement of the lowest price is not an offer to sell
why: Giving price information only invites offers; it isn't a promise to sell.

q: In an IPO, what is the company's prospectus?
options: An invitation to offer; investors' bids are offers and allotment is acceptance
An offer that every applicant can accept
why: That's why oversubscribed bidders can get fewer shares with no breach claim.

q: An auction house withdraws a car it advertised; a collector sues for his ₹18,000 airfare. Likely result?
options: He wins, the ad was an offer
He loses: an auction ad is an invitation to offer (Harris v Nickerson)
why: No offer, so no contract and no claim for travel expenses.

q: What did Fitch v Snedaker decide?
options: You can't accept an offer you don't know about
why: Acting without knowing of a reward isn't acceptance of it.

q: A seller writes: 'If I don't hear from you by Monday, you're buying my laptop for ₹35,000.' The buyer stays silent. Contract?
options: Only if the price is fair
Yes, if the laptop is new
why: The offeror can't force acceptance through the other side's silence.

q: India's CCPA asked platforms in June 2025 to remove 'dark patterns' like subscription traps. Which acceptance rule does this echo?
options: Real acceptance needs a clear, communicated yes, not inertia or pre-ticked boxes
Acceptance can be implied from silence
Acceptance must be in stamp paper
why: Consent must be informed and communicated, not engineered through design tricks.

q: Under Indian law, must consideration come from the promisee?
options: No, it may come from the promisee or any other person
why: Section 2(d), applied in Chinnaya v Ramayya.

q: A sells his ₹2 lakh car to B for ₹50,000, willingly. Is the contract void?
options: Only if B is a relative
Yes, the price must be market value
No, consideration need not be adequate if consent is free
why: Courts don't judge the bargain, though a shockingly low price may hint at a consent problem.

q: A neighbour orally promises you ₹10,000 'because you're like my son', then refuses. Can you sue?
options: Only if a witness heard it
No: no consideration, and the exception needs writing, registration and near relatives
Yes, love and affection is enough
why: Section 25's love-and-affection exception has strict conditions.

q: What is the legal status of an agreement with a minor?
options: Void from the start (void ab initio)
Valid if the minor lies about age
why: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose (1903); a minor also can't ratify it later.

q: A minor buys ₹3,000 of textbooks on credit. Can the seller recover the money?
options: Yes, but only from the minor's property, as these are necessaries
why: Section 68: a reasonable price for necessaries comes from the minor's estate.

q: A start-up signs up 16-year-olds to a paid app plan with no parent involved. What's the risk?
options: The contracts are void and, under the DPDP Rules, processing their data needs verifiable parental consent
why: Contract law and data law both treat under-18s as unable to give binding consent.

q: A contract obtained by coercion is…
options: Voidable at the option of the coerced party
why: Section 19: the victim may cancel it, or choose to keep it.

q: A spiritual guru persuades a devoted follower to transfer her ₹40 lakh flat to his trust. Most likely ground?
why: Misuse of a position of trust and dominance is undue influence.

q: In 'digital arrest' scams, fraudsters threaten victims with arrest on video calls until they transfer money. Which concept fits best?
options: Coercion: consent obtained by threat, and also a crime
why: Money paid under threat isn't given with free consent.

q: What is a voidable contract?
options: One with no effect from the start
A valid contract that one party may choose to cancel
why: Typically arises where consent wasn't free: coercion, fraud, undue influence.

q: Two friends bet ₹1,000 on the IPL final. The agreement is…
why: Wagers are void, though not every void agreement is a crime.

q: After the 2025 online-gaming law banned real-money games, Dream11 stopped paid contests. Why couldn't such agreements continue?
options: Their object became unlawful, so agreements to play for money lost legal force
why: A lawful object is essential; once the law forbids it, the agreement can't stand.

q: What is puffery in advertising?
options: Vague, exaggerated praise no reasonable consumer takes literally
why: 'World's best pizza' is puffery; specific claims are not.

q: A shampoo ad says 'Reduces hair fall by 90% in 2 weeks'. This is…
options: A factual claim that must be substantiated
why: Specific, measurable claims need evidence.

q: In 2024 the Supreme Court pulled up Patanjali over ads claiming to treat diseases. Why weren't these just puffery?
options: Because 'cures' disease is a specific health claim that needs proof
Because the price was too high
why: Health and performance claims are treated as statements of fact.

q: What is anticipatory breach?
options: Breach before the due date, by refusal or conduct making performance impossible
why: Section 39: the innocent party can sue at once.

q: Peter agrees to sell John a guitar on 10 March, but sells it to Oliver on 7 March. What can John do?
options: Treat it as anticipatory breach and sue right away
Buy it from Oliver at Peter's cost automatically
why: Conduct made performance impossible before the due date.

q: A supplier says in March it won't deliver in June. What's the smart business response?
options: Treat the contract as ended, source elsewhere now, and claim the extra cost
why: Acting early mitigates loss; waiting only adds risk.

q: Under Section 73, which losses can be claimed?
options: Losses arising naturally from the breach, or that both sides knew were likely
why: Remote, indirect losses aren't covered (Hadley v Baxendale).

q: A seller fails to deliver 100 bags of rice at ₹2,000; the buyer buys elsewhere at ₹2,300. Damages?
why: Market price minus contract price: (2,300 − 2,000) × 100.

q: A contract says '₹2,000 per day of delay'; the builder is 10 days late. What will an Indian court award?
why: India awards reasonable compensation not exceeding the named amount.

q: What does quantum meruit mean?
options: 'As much as earned': reasonable pay for work done before the other side stopped it
A court order to stop an act
why: It prevents the other party getting the work for free.

q: A seller refuses to hand over a rare 1965 vintage car you agreed to buy. Best remedy?
options: Specific performance, since the car is unique
why: Where money can't replace the thing, courts can order performance.

q: A rescinds a contract after B's breach but has already received ₹50,000 of B's goods. What must A do?
options: Keep the goods as a penalty
Return the benefit (Sec 65) while claiming compensation for loss (Sec 75)
why: Rescission requires giving back what you received.

q: Is consideration needed to create an agency?
why: An unpaid friend selling your bike is still your agent.

q: A transporter sells a trader's mangoes before they rot when the truck is stuck for days. Was he authorised?
why: He acted as a prudent person would to protect the principal from loss.

q: A company let its sales head sign orders for two years, then calls his ₹8 lakh order unauthorised under an internal limit the supplier never knew. Who likely wins?
options: The sales head personally pays all
why: The company's conduct made the authority appear real to the third party.

q: What does 'delegatus non potest delegare' mean?
options: A delegate cannot delegate, unless custom or the nature of the work allows it
why: Section 190: agency is built on personal trust.

q: A buys goods for B without authority; B later resells them to C. What has B done?
why: Implied ratification (Sec 197).

q: A principal wants to ratify an unauthorised ₹5 lakh deal but drop its penalty clause. Can he?
options: No, ratifying part ratifies the whole (Sec 199)
why: Ratification is all or nothing.

q: Must a principal indemnify an agent for a criminal act done on the principal's instructions?
options: Only if the agent is a minor
why: Illegality defeats the duty to indemnify.

q: A gives B authority to sell A's land and pay B's own dues from the proceeds. Can A revoke it?
options: No, it's an agency coupled with interest (Sec 202)
why: The agent's interest makes the agency irrevocable to his prejudice.

q: SEBI's 2026 order in the Axis MF front-running case barred a former chief dealer for 7 years. Which agent duty does front-running break?
options: Loyalty: no conflict and no secret profit (Ss 215–216)
Duty to render accounts on time
Duty to follow trade custom on credit
why: Using the principal's position to profit privately is the core breach of agency trust.

q: Under Sec 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act, which of these is NOT 'goods'?
options: An actionable claim like a debt owed to you
Growing crops agreed to be cut
why: Goods exclude money and actionable claims.

q: A farmer agrees in March to sell wheat he'll harvest in May. This is…
options: An agreement to sell future goods
why: Future goods can only be the subject of an agreement to sell.

q: You buy a specific ₹50,000 sofa and leave it at the shop; a flood destroys it before delivery. Who bears the loss?
options: You, since ownership passed and risk follows ownership
The shop, since it had the sofa
why: Sec 20 and 26: risk follows ownership, not possession (absent negligence or a contrary term).

q: Breach of a warranty gives the buyer…
options: The right to reject the goods
why: A warranty is collateral to the main purpose (Sec 12(3)).

q: You order 'basmati rice' and get ordinary rice in a basmati bag. Which implied condition is broken?
why: Goods sold by description must match it.

q: In Sep 2025 a consumer commission ordered Mercedes-Benz to refund over ₹1.78 crore for a defective new EQS. Why a refund, not just repairs?
options: A new car that can't be fixed breaks the condition of merchantable quality, allowing rejection
why: Breach of a condition lets the buyer reject the goods and recover the price.

q: What does caveat emptor mean?
why: Section 16: the buyer should check the goods suit their purpose.

q: A buyer tells a paint dealer the wall gets heavy rain, buys his recommendation, and it peels in a month. Is the dealer protected by caveat emptor?
options: Only if the paint was cheap
Only if the buyer is a minor
why: The buyer disclosed the purpose and relied on the dealer's skill.

q: In 2024 Hong Kong flagged ethylene oxide in some MDH and Everest spice mixes. Why doesn't caveat emptor leave shoppers on their own here?
options: Food must be merchantable and wholesome, and buyers can't test it themselves
why: The merchantable-quality and wholesomeness exceptions protect buyers.

q: When can an unpaid seller use stoppage in transit?
options: When the buyer is insolvent and goods are still with a carrier
why: Section 50: it extends the lien while goods are in transit.

q: A seller still holds goods sold on 15 days' credit; the credit has expired unpaid. Which right fits?
options: Lien: keep the goods until paid (Sec 47)
why: Lien applies while goods are in the seller's possession.

q: A buyer refuses 100 cartons of mangoes at ₹500 each; they will spoil in days and resell at ₹400. What can the seller claim?
options: Resell them and claim the ₹10,000 shortfall
₹50,000 in full and keep the mangoes
why: Perishable goods may be resold (Sec 54): (500 − 400) × 100.

q: Business ethics is best described as…
options: Applying ideas of right and wrong to business decisions
why: It covers everyday choices like pricing, selling, hiring and reporting, not just law or charity.

q: A shopkeeper uses honest weights even though customers can't check. Which feature of ethics does this show?
options: Honesty as a voluntary code of conduct
why: Doing right when no one is watching is ethics in practice.

q: FTX's founder was sentenced to 25 years in 2024 after customers lost about $8 billion. Which ethical failure lay at the heart of it?
options: Dishonesty with people who trusted the firm with their money
why: Secretly using customer deposits broke the most basic duty of honesty.

q: What is the key difference between law and ethics?
options: Law is compulsory and enforced; ethics is largely voluntary and goes beyond the law
Law covers grey areas, ethics doesn't
why: Law is the floor; ethics asks what is right.

q: A landlord legally raises a student's rent sharply in exam month because the contract allows it. This is…
why: Allowed by the contract, but it exploits the student's position.

q: A 2024 report said Nestlé's Cerelac had added sugar in India but not in similar UK products. Why is this an ethics question even if Indian rules were met?
options: Because a double standard across countries raises fairness concerns the law doesn't settle
why: Compliance and ethics differ; fair treatment of all customers matters.

q: Which is a business reason for being ethical?
options: Long-term survival, customer trust and fewer penalties
why: Unethical gains are short-lived; trust compounds.

q: A repair shop overcharges ₹800 by fitting a used part. What's the likely long-run effect?
options: Lost trust, fewer repeat visits and bad reviews
why: The one-time gain costs future business.

q: In 2024 the RBI barred Paytm Payments Bank from taking new deposits, citing persistent non-compliance. What lesson does this teach?
options: Ignoring compliance can cost a business its core activities, far more than compliance costs
why: Persistent failures led to the loss of key functions almost overnight.

q: What is the 'newspaper test'?
options: Asking whether you'd be comfortable if your decision were front-page news
why: If you'd hate it to be public, it probably isn't right.

q: You're told to make sure the CEO's under-qualified nephew is hired. Which values clash?
options: Fairness and merit vs loyalty and self-protection
why: That's a classic workplace ethical dilemma from the module.

q: Your manager asks you to approve a medicine batch that failed a quality test, to avoid delay. Best response?
options: Refuse, present the evidence, and escalate through the ethics or vigil channel if pressured
Ask a colleague to sign instead
why: Public safety outweighs speed; the Coldrif tragedy shows the stakes.

q: Utilitarianism judges an action by…
options: Its consequences: the greatest good for the greatest number
why: Associated with Bentham and Mill.

q: ₹50,000 can buy an AC for 20 staff or water purifiers for 2,000 students. What would a utilitarian choose?
why: Far more people benefit for the same money.

q: What is the main weakness of a pure utilitarian approach to layoffs?
options: It can justify harming a minority if the majority gains
why: Outcomes must be checked against rights and fair process.

q: Kant's categorical imperative says…
options: Act only on rules you could will as universal laws, and treat people as ends
why: Duty ethics focuses on principles, not results.

q: A manager promotes a friend through a secret process over a better-qualified colleague. Which justice is violated?
why: The process itself was unfair.

q: Karnataka's 2025 gig workers law set a 1–5% welfare fee on aggregators and notice before termination. Which ethical idea does this reflect most?
options: Rights and justice: fair security and process for workers
why: It protects workers' rights, not just customers' low prices.

q: Gandhian trusteeship says a businessperson should…
options: See themselves as a trustee of wealth, to be used for society's good
why: Wealth is held in trust, with harmony between capital and labour.

q: A leader asks 'what would an honest, fair person do here?' rather than checking rules or numbers. Which approach is this?
why: Virtue ethics focuses on character.

q: A promoter donates ₹50 crore to a hospital but underpays factory workers. Is that trusteeship?
options: Only if the hospital is free
No, trusteeship covers fair treatment of labour every day, not just donations
why: Charity can't cover for unfair operations.

q: At Kohlberg's first stage, people follow rules mainly to…
why: Pre-conventional reasoning centres on self.

q: An employee reports fraud only because 'company rules say I must'. Which stage?
why: Conventional level: duty to rules and the system.

q: Deloitte's 2024 survey found half of Gen Zs had turned down assignments on ethical grounds. In Kohlberg's terms this reflects…
options: Higher-stage, principled reasoning even at personal cost
why: Choosing on principle is post-conventional.

q: Which is an example of deliberate deception at work?
options: Taking credit for a colleague's work
why: The module lists credit-stealing, fake sick leave and sabotage.

q: A trainee runs a mouse-jiggler app to look active for 2 hours a day. What is it?
options: Misuse of company time and deception
why: Wells Fargo fired staff for exactly this in 2024.

q: Reps mis-sell insurance under extreme targets. Whose ethics problem is it?
options: Both the reps' and the organisation's target design and culture
why: Fixing it needs realistic targets and quality checks, not just blame.

q: A conflict of interest arises when…
options: Personal gain could improperly influence a decision made for someone else
why: Hiding and acting on it is the breach.

q: Your close friend bids for a contract you're evaluating. What should you do first?
options: Disclose the relationship and step out of the evaluation
why: Disclose, recuse, let independent people decide.

q: In 2025 a tribunal found substance in an alleged 'quid pro quo' linking a ₹300 crore ICICI loan and ₹64 crore to a firm tied to the ex-CEO's husband. What principle was at stake?
options: Avoiding conflicts of interest in lending decisions
why: Personal interest must never shape decisions made for the bank.

q: Internal whistleblowing means reporting wrongdoing to…
options: People inside the organisation, like management or the audit committee
why: External whistleblowing goes to regulators or the press.

q: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 requires listed companies to set up a vigil mechanism?
why: Section 177 covers the vigil mechanism.

q: An employee's report of fraud is brushed off and the fraud continues. What's the right next step?
options: Escalate through the formal vigil mechanism, then the regulator if needed
why: Use internal routes first, then external ones if they fail.

q: Which are the core principles of corporate governance?
why: They make leaders answerable to shareholders and stakeholders.

q: At least what share of a listed Indian company's board must be independent directors?
why: Independent directors are the board's internal check.

q: IndusInd Bank's 2025 derivative accounting lapses had built up over years. Which governance mechanism should have caught them earlier?
options: A strong audit committee and internal controls
why: Audit committees must probe complex areas, not just sign off.

q: Milton Friedman said the social responsibility of business is to…
options: Increase its profits, within the rules of the game
why: Within open, free competition and without deception or fraud.

q: A firm sets goals for staff well-being, supplier fairness and emissions alongside profit. Which theory?
why: It balances everyone affected.

q: Which is a weakness of pure profit maximisation?
options: It ignores risk, time value of money and intangibles like quality and reputation
why: Module 2 lists these disadvantages.

q: Carroll's CSR pyramid, from the base, is…
why: Profitability is the foundation; philanthropy is the top.

q: A company sets 'cut water use per unit by 15% in two years' and reports yearly. Which good CSR practice?
why: Real CSR is integrated and measured.

q: Google reported in 2024 that its emissions rose 48% since 2019 despite a net-zero 2030 goal. What does this show about CSR?
options: Pledges must be matched by measured, honestly reported progress
why: Credibility comes from reporting, even when numbers go the wrong way.

q: Under Section 135, the minimum CSR spend is…
options: 2% of average net profit of the preceding three years
why: It uses the three-year average, not the current year.

q: Net profits of ₹40, ₹50 and ₹60 crore over the last three years mean a minimum CSR spend of…
why: Average ₹50 crore × 2% = ₹1 crore.

q: A company spends its CSR money on a gym for its own staff. Does it count as CSR?
options: No, activities benefiting only its own employees don't qualify
why: CSR must go to Schedule VII activities for the public.
